content: Joint pain, also referred to as arthralgia (derived from the Greek words arthromeaning joint and -algos meaning pain), arises from a variety of causes. These include trauma, infections, inflammation, degeneration of bone and/or cartilage, allergic reactions to medications, and deposition of crystals within the joint. It is important to distinguish between the terms arthralgia and arthritis, as the former is used when the joint pain is non-inflammatory in origin, while the latter is reserved for inflammatory causes. As an orthopedic resident, it is your responsibility to evaluate patients presenting with joint pain. This involves localizing the source of the pain and identifying the underlying pathophysiological cause(s). To achieve this, you must consider a broad range of differential diagnoses and systematically narrow them down to determine the primary cause. A thorough past medical history is essential in this process. Causes of Arthralgia: Arthralgia can result from a wide range of conditions, including degenerative and destructive processes (e.g., arthritis and sports injuries), inflammation of the tissues surrounding the joint (e.g., bursitis), infections, or even as a reaction to vaccinations. Broadly, joint pain can be categorized into three main causes: 1. Inflammatory Arthritis: This type of arthritis is primarily caused by inflammation affecting joint structures such as the synovium, synovial cavity, and entheses. 2. Non-inflammatory Arthritis: This form of arthritis arises from structural or mechanical changes in the joint rather than inflammation. 3. Arthralgia: This refers to joint tenderness without any detectable joint abnormalities. Life-Threatening Causes: Certain conditions causing joint pain can be life-threatening if left untreated, potentially leading to death or permanent disability within 24 hours.
